subtitle: "A simulation-validation case: a whole-record fit reproduces a Fantasia subject's heart-rate variability"

> **What this case shows** — a closed-loop physiological model is only credible if,
> *fit to a real recording*, it reproduces that recording — not just if it recovers
> its own parameters on synthetic data. Here the **closed-loop cardiovascular
> state-space model** (a damped Mayer oscillator driving the heart period, plus a
> respiratory RSA term) is fit to a **real** RR-interval record (PhysioNet
> **Fantasia**, young subject f1y03) by whole-record Bayesian inference. The fit is
> stable and physiological (Mayer damping ρ = 0.75, interior — not railed) and it
> reproduces both the record's overall variability (**RR SD 45.8 vs the real 47.5
> ms**) and its low-/high-frequency autonomic balance (**LF/HF 5.98 vs the real
> 6.86**). This is the **validation-against-reality** tier, distinct from the
> synthetic-data recovery that only *verifies* the estimator. **How to read it** —
> left, the real and fitted-model HRV power spectra, both carrying the Mayer (LF)
> and respiratory (HF) peaks; right, the real and model RR tachograms.

::: {.callout-tip title="The recipe you'll learn"}
**Workflow** — to validate a closed-loop model against real data: measure the real
signal's second-order structure (its variance and its LF/HF spectral balance),
**fit** the model to the whole record by Bayesian inference, then check the fitted
model reproduces that variance and balance.
**Way of thinking** — "the sampler recovers the true parameters on a simulated
record" is **verification of the estimator**; "the model, fit to a subject,
reproduces that subject's real HRV" is **validation of the model** — a different,
stronger claim. It is a claim about the **second-order** (spectral) structure, not
the exact stochastic RR series.
**Ecosystem usage** — `cardioStateSpace()` / `personalizeCardioWaveform()`
(PhysioTwin) for the whole-record fit; `particleMCMC()` / `particleGibbs()` for the
general nonlinear case; the same fit-then-compare protocol validates any state-space
twin against a real record.
:::

## Proposition

The closed-loop model, fit to a real RR record, reproduces that record's HRV: fit to
Fantasia f1y03 it reaches a physiological solution (ρ = 0.75) that reproduces the RR
SD (45.8 vs 47.5 ms) and the LF/HF autonomic balance (5.98 vs 6.86), with the record
carrying a separated Mayer (0.10 Hz) and respiratory (0.18 Hz) rhythm.

## Question & goal

**The question is model credibility, not code correctness.** A twin's in-silico
predictions are only worth trusting if the model matches reality. Recovering the
true parameters from a *simulated* record verifies the *sampler*; it says nothing
about whether the *model* matches a heart. We ask the harder question: fit the
closed-loop model to a real subject's RR record and see whether it reproduces that
subject's actual heart-rate variability.

## Challenge & approach

We take a 600-beat resting RR segment of Fantasia record f1y03, measure its HRV
(SD, LF/HF band powers, and the Mayer/respiratory spectral peaks), and **fit** the
closed-loop `cardioStateSpace` model to the whole series with
`personalizeCardioWaveform()` — an exact Kalman likelihood (the model is
linear-Gaussian) sampled by Metropolis. We then generate synthetic RR from the
fitted model and compare its HRV, averaged over realisations, with the real one.

## Data

**Fantasia f1y03** (Iyengar et al., PhysioNet) — a 600-beat resting RR segment @
250 Hz from a young healthy subject. Details in
[`artifacts/data_sources.json`](artifacts/data_sources.json).

## Results

![The real HRV power spectrum (blue) and the fitted closed-loop model's spectrum
(red), both carrying the low-frequency Mayer peak and the high-frequency
respiratory peak (grey dashed = LF/HF band edges); right, the real (blue) and model
(red) RR tachograms.](artifacts/figure.png)

*How to read this:* fitting the closed loop to the whole record — not to summary
statistics — recovers a single physiological parameter set whose generated HRV
matches the real record's variance and its low-/high-frequency balance.

| quantity | real | fitted model |
|---|---|---|
| RR SD (ms) | 47.5 | **45.8** |
| LF/HF ratio | 6.86 | **5.98** |
| Mayer (LF) peak | 0.10 Hz | — |
| respiratory (HF) peak | 0.18 Hz | — |
| fitted Mayer damping ρ | — | 0.75 (interior) |

## Conclusion

The closed-loop cardiovascular model, fit to a real subject's RR record by
whole-record Bayesian inference, reproduces that subject's heart-rate variability —
its variance and its autonomic balance — at a stable, physiological fit. The model
is **validated against reality**, not merely verified on synthetic data. The
transferable takeaway: **fit the whole record, then check the model reproduces a
second-order structure it was not directly handed — and be explicit that the claim
is about the spectrum, not the exact series.**

## Open questions

- The model is a linear idealisation with free LF/HF amplitudes, so matching the
  LF/HF ratio is partly structural, and it does **not** fit every record (e.g.
  MIT-BIH record 100 and some Fantasia subjects, whose Mayer/RSA peaks are not
  separated, rail the fit at its bounds). A higher-order or nonlinear closed loop
  fit by `particleMCMC()` / `particleGibbs()`, validated across many subjects and
  conditions, would capture those and map the domain of applicability. *Documented,
  not escalated.*

## Using this in your own analysis

| step | function | package |
|---|---|---|
| closed-loop state-space model | `cardioStateSpace()` | PhysioTwin |
| whole-record Bayesian fit | `personalizeCardioWaveform()` | PhysioTwin |
| general nonlinear fit | `particleMCMC()` / `particleGibbs()` | PhysioTwin |
